newsitem.title: USA: Women who get epidurals subject newborns to tests - study.
newsitem.headline: Women who get epidurals subject newborns to tests - study.

text.p: Babies born to mothers who received an epidural to ease labour pains were three times as likely to be subjected to discomforting tests for infection after birth, researchers said Monday.

Newborns of mothers who chose to receive the pain-killing shot were no more likely to actually have the infection than other babies, the study found. But epidurals have been linked to maternal fevers during labour, a possible sign of infection, and that led doctors to order tests on the babies anyway.

In the study of 1,657 births at Boston's Brigham and Women's Hospitals, 34 percent of babies born to mothers who got the epidural needed an evaluation for potentially dangerous sepsis, compared to 10 percent of the babies born to mothers who did not have the shot.

Actual infections were rare in both groups. But more than 14 percent of the women who received the pain-killing shot developed a temperature of more than 100.4 degrees (38 Celsius), against only 1 percent who developed fevers among those who did not get the shot.
Newborns whose mothers received epidurals also were 10 times more likely to be treated with antibiotics because doctors were concerned about infection.

No studies have been done to show the effect on the foetus of elevated maternal temperature, study co-author Ellice Lieberman of Harvard Medical School wrote in the article that appeared in the journal Pediatrics.
